Two-stage p-tau217 reflex testing reduces the modeled PET gray zone

In external validation among 1,644 A4/LEARN participants, a p-tau217 gatekeeper followed by a multimarker reflex model improved gray-zone AUC from 0.719 to 0.793, reduced PET referral from 35.9% to 24.3%, and classified 90.7% without PET.

Key quantitative results: Full-model AUC was 0.915 (95% CI, 0.859–0.961) in ADNI and 0.879 (95% CI, 0.861–0.895) in external A4/LEARN validation.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42/40Sequential testing

Added October 20, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/acn3.70560; PMID:42897700

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

GRAD routes a p-tau217 probability of 0.25 to 0.75 to a reflex model using p-tau217, Aβ42/40, GFAP, APOE ε4, age, and a tau-amyloid divergence term. External gray-zone discrimination improved and modeled PET use fell, but calibration shifted across cohorts and the reflex stage alone did not meet recommended performance for replacing amyloid PET.

Study design

Investigators developed the two-stage GRAD algorithm in 145 cognitively impaired ADNI participants and externally validated the locked model in 1,644 cognitively unimpaired A4/LEARN participants. Amyloid PET was the reference standard: florbetapir SUVR greater than 1.11 in ADNI and at least 20 Centiloids in A4/LEARN. Probabilities below 0.25 or above 0.75 were resolved by p-tau217 alone; the gray zone entered an L2-regularized multimarker model.

Key quantitative results

  • Full-model AUC was 0.915 (95% CI, 0.859–0.961) in ADNI and 0.879 (95% CI, 0.861–0.895) in external A4/LEARN validation.
  • Among 630 external gray-zone participants, the reflex model improved AUC from 0.719 with p-tau217 alone to 0.793 (p<0.001), increased correct classification without PET from 41.4% to 56.2%, and reduced PET referral from 35.9% to 24.3%.
  • Overall, 89.0% of ADNI and 90.7% of A4/LEARN participants were classified without PET. External sensitivity was 76.7%, specificity 88.6%, PPV 93.9%, and NPV 62.3%.
  • Calibration did not fully transfer: the external intercept was +0.93, with mean predicted risk 57.5% versus observed amyloid prevalence 69.6%.
  • Modeled testing costs were 44%–52% lower than p-tau217 screening followed by PET for every gray-zone result; this was an economic simulation, not a prospective utilization study.

What changed

A peer-reviewed, externally tested reflex architecture now quantifies how a second blood-based stage can shrink the p-tau217 gray zone while preserving PET for residual uncertainty.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence because the model was locked and externally validated against amyloid PET in a large independent cohort. Clinical utility remains unproven because routing decisions, patient outcomes, and real-world costs were modeled rather than prospectively tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support reflex testing as a research and implementation strategy, not a replacement for confirmatory imaging. The external calibration shift, 62.3% NPV, and below-replacement performance of the reflex stage require local validation before individual treatment or enrollment decisions.

Field medical relevance

Directly addresses common MSL questions about p-tau217 gray zones, sequential testing, cross-platform transport, residual PET demand, prevalence effects, and the distinction between discrimination and calibration.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The model was developed with Lumipulse and Janssen p-tau217 measurements and transported to Lilly MSD p-tau217, with platform harmonization based on cohort-specific reference distributions. The cross-platform result is encouraging, but the thresholds are not directly transferable laboratory cutoffs and require setting-specific calibration.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The workflow could reduce confirmatory PET demand if prospectively validated, but the publication creates no new authorization, availability, reimbursement, coverage, or ordering pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does GRAD replace amyloid PET?
No. The authors retain PET for residual uncertainty, and the external reflex stage achieved 66.7% sensitivity and 80.0% specificity, below the recommended benchmark for replacing PET.
Are the 0.25 and 0.75 values laboratory concentration cutoffs?
No. They are model probabilities after platform harmonization, not transferable pg/mL cutoffs.
Did the cost savings occur in clinical practice?
No. Costs were modeled using cohort routing rates and assumed unit prices.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Small development cohort and only 49 development gray-zone cases
  • External cohort was cognitively unimpaired, unlike the cognitively impaired development cohort
  • Cross-platform harmonization used cohort-specific reference distributions
  • External calibration shifted materially
  • No prospective clinical-utility, decision-impact, or health-system implementation trial
  • Cost results depend on assumed prices and modeled routing
